warmup.q: A payments topic has 6 partitions and a group of 6 consumers. Your service sends an authorization and then a capture for acct-42, both with key acct-42, from one producer. Which is true?
options: The capture can be processed first, because six consumers work in parallel
Both go to the same partition, so the one consumer that reads it sees the authorization first
Kafka orders every record in the topic by timestamp, so the order is safe
Order is kept only if you set the partition number on each record yourself
warmup.why: The key hashes to one partition, and a partition is a log read in order by one consumer of the group. Six consumers in parallel is the tempting answer, but each partition still has just one reader per group. Kafka keeps no order across partitions, by timestamp or otherwise, and you don't need explicit partitions: the key already pins the account to one.

sections.h: The producer picks the partition, and the key decides it
sections.html:
A topic with 6 partitions is six separate logs (lesson 3 of this track). When your payment service calls send(), one of the six has to get the record. The broker doesn't choose. The producer does, inside your JVM, before the record leaves it. Then it sends the record to that partition's leader, the broker that holds the partition's main copy (lesson 4 of this track).

What should the rule be? The simplest one is round robin: record 1 to partition 0, record 2 to partition 1, and so on. It spreads the load evenly and breaks payments at once. The authorization for acct-42 lands in partition 0 and its capture in partition 1. Two consumers read those partitions at their own pace, and the capture can be processed first. A ledger that sees a capture with no authorization rejects it, or worse, books it twice.

So the rule needs one property: every record of one account goes to the same partition. Then that account's records sit in one log, in the order they were appended, and lesson 2 showed that a log keeps its order. The rule must also work with no coordination, because you run eight instances of the payment service and none of them asks the others.

The Partitioning track had the same problem with database rows and the same answer, and a hash function gives it here too. It turns any bytes into a number. The same bytes always give the same number, and bytes that differ by one character give unrelated numbers, so keys spread out. The record's key is the input. It is optional, and Kafka itself gives it no meaning; you choose it, and for payments the account id is the usual choice.

The default partitioner in the Java client does four steps:

  1. Serialize the key. StringSerializer turns "acct-17" into its 7 UTF-8 bytes.
  2. Hash the bytes with murmur2, a fast 32-bit hash. For acct-17 it gives -1871546916.
  3. Clear the sign bit (hash & 0x7fffffff), because a Java int can be negative and a partition number can't. -1871546916 becomes 275936732.
  4. Take the remainder by the partition count: 275936732 % 6 = 2.

So acct-17 goes to partition 2 of 6, from every producer, every time. Note step 3: it is not Math.abs. Math.abs(-1871546916) % 6 is 0, so a test or a tool that predicts partitions with Math.abs gets most keys with a negative hash wrong. Lesson 4's AcksDemo reported acct-17 in partition 2 of 3, and you can now check why: 275936732 % 3 is 2.

The rule lives in each client library, not in Kafka. librdkafka, the C library behind Confluent's Python, Go and .NET clients, hashes keys with CRC32 by default. A Go service and a Java service writing the same key can pick different partitions unless the Go side sets partitioner=murmur2_random. Two ways skip the hash entirely: a ProducerRecord built with an explicit partition number goes to that partition, and partitioner.class plugs in your own rule.

try.title: Hash a key by hand, then let the producer do it
steps: From the labs folder, start the broker: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait. Then create a topic with 6 partitions: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic accounts --partitions 6.
Run the demo (command below). For four keys it prints the murmur2 hash, the hash with its sign bit cleared, the remainder by the partition count, and the partition the real producer chose.
acct-18 differs from acct-17 in one character. Predict: will its hash be close? Then run the demo again with -Pargs=acct-18 added.
Keep the broker running for the next Try-its.

code.title: PartitionForDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.msg.l05.demo; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord; import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer; import org.apache.kafka.common.utils.Utils; import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * For each key: the murmur2 hash, the hash made positive, the partition that arithmetic gives, * and the partition the real producer chose when it sent a record with that key to the topic "accounts". */ public class PartitionForDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { List<String> keys = args.length > 0 ? List.of(args) : List.of("acct-17", "acct-42", "acct-99", "card-1"); Map<String, Object> config = Map.of( "bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092", // env/kafka.yml "key.serializer", StringSerializer.class, "value.serializer", StringSerializer.class); try (var producer = new KafkaProducer<String, String>(config)) { int n = producer.partitionsFor("accounts").size(); System.out.printf("topic accounts has %d partitions%n", n); System.out.printf("%-9s %12s %11s %5s %s%n", "key", "murmur2", "positive", "% " + n, "producer chose"); for (String key : keys) { int hash = Utils.murmur2(key.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)); // the bytes StringSerializer sends int positive = Utils.toPositive(hash); // hash & 0x7fffffff int chosen = producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("accounts", key, "auth 10.00 EUR")).get().partition(); System.out.printf("%-9s %12d %11d %5d partition %d%n", key, hash, positive, positive % n, chosen); } } } }

alt.html: package sfz.msg.l05.demo import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer import org.apache.kafka.common.utils.Utils /** * For each key: the murmur2 hash, the hash made positive, the partition that arithmetic gives, * and the partition the real producer chose when it sent a record with that key to the topic "accounts". */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val keys = args.toList().ifEmpty { listOf("acct-17", "acct-42", "acct-99", "card-1") } val config = mapOf<String, Any>( "bootstrap.servers" to "localhost:9092", // env/kafka.yml "key.serializer" to StringSerializer::class.java, "value.serializer" to StringSerializer::class.java, ) KafkaProducer<String, String>(config).use { producer -> val n = producer.partitionsFor("accounts").size println("topic accounts has $n partitions") println("%-9s %12s %11s %5s %s".format("key", "murmur2", "positive", "% $n", "producer chose")) for (key in keys) { val hash = Utils.murmur2(key.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8)) // the bytes StringSerializer sends val positive = Utils.toPositive(hash) // hash and 0x7fffffff val chosen = producer.send(ProducerRecord("accounts", key, "auth 10.00 EUR")).get().partition() println("%-9s %12d %11d %5d partition %d".format(key, hash, positive, positive % n, chosen)) } } }

try.expect:
topic accounts has 6 partitions
key            murmur2    positive   % 6   producer chose
acct-17    -1871546916   275936732     2   partition 2
acct-42    -1294421753   853061895     3   partition 3
acct-99    -1758549442   388934206     4   partition 4
card-1       830907359   830907359     5   partition 5

The remainder and the producer's choice agree on every line, and you get the same numbers: the hash depends only on the key's bytes. Three of the four hashes are negative; clearing the sign bit turns -1871546916 into 275936732, which is 2^31 minus 1871546916, not its absolute value. acct-18 hashes to 212957696, nothing like its neighbour, and still lands in partition 2. With 6 partitions any two keys share one about one time in six. (The Kotlin demo prints the same table.)

refs.title: Confluent: the importance of standardized hashing across producers

sections.h: One key keeps its order; the topic as a whole has none
sections.html:
Records with the same key go to the same partition, and a partition is a log that only appends at its end. So if one producer sends the authorization for acct-42 before its capture, the leader appends them in that order, and every consumer of that partition reads them in that order. That is the whole ordering promise: order within one partition, so order per key. It is also what the queue of lesson 1 could not give its competing consumers: within a group, each partition has one reader at a time, so one account's records are never in flight on two consumers at once.

Across partitions there is no order at all. Partition 0 and partition 3 are two files on maybe two brokers, and nothing records that a record in one was sent before a record in the other. A consumer that reads several partitions gets them in whatever order its fetches come back: a run from partition 3, then a run from partition 0. Step through it below.

Can you get global order? Only with one partition, and lesson 3 of this track put a number on that: one partition means one consumer per group, about 500 payments a second if each takes 2 ms. Almost no payment system needs global order. What it needs is order per account, or per payment, and a key gives you that while the load spreads across partitions.

Two limits on the promise. First, it is the order in which records reach the leader. Two instances of your service that send events for the same account at the same moment race each other, and the leader appends whichever arrives first. If the business order matters, one instance should own each account, or the event should carry a version number the consumer checks. Second, retries can reorder records inside one producer. Lesson 6 of this track shows how, and how the idempotent producer, on by default, prevents it.

The Try-it below sends 1,000 payments for 10 accounts into the 6 partitions of accounts and reads them back. Look at how the 10 keys spread. Partition 4 gets three accounts and partition 1 gets one. With 10 keys, hashing is lumpy; with 100,000 accounts each partition gets close to a sixth.

stepper.title: Keys pick the log, and order lives inside one log

try.title: 1,000 payments, 10 accounts, 6 partitions
steps: Run KeyOrderDemo (command below). It sends seq 0 to 999 with the key cycling through acct-1 to acct-10, then reads the records back with one consumer and checks the order.
Before you look: how many partitions will each account use, and will the whole stream come back in send order?
Look at the in send order: line. Keyed records follow their keys, so the partition changes on almost every record.

code.title: KeyOrderDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.msg.l05.demo; import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.ConsumerRecord; import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.KafkaConsumer; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.RecordMetadata; import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition; import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer; import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.*; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** * Sends 1,000 payments for acct-1 .. acct-10 in turn to the topic "accounts", then reads them back with one consumer. * Each value starts with its send order (seq). Pass a mode: keys (the default), no-keys or ignore-keys. */ public class KeyOrderDemo { static final String TOPIC = "accounts"; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "keys"; Map<String, Object> common = Map.of("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092", "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class); Map<String, Object> producerConfig = new HashMap<>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092", "key.serializer", StringSerializer.class, "value.serializer", StringSerializer.class)); if (mode.equals("ignore-keys")) producerConfig.put("partitioner.ignore.keys", true); // 1. note where every partition ends now, so we read back only this run's records Map<TopicPartition, Long> start; try (var consumer = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(common)) { List<TopicPartition> tps = consumer.partitionsFor(TOPIC).stream() .map(p -> new TopicPartition(TOPIC, p.partition())).toList(); start = consumer.endOffsets(tps); } // 2. send seq 0..999; the key cycles through the 10 accounts (or is null) List<Integer> sentTo = new ArrayList<>(); try (var producer = new KafkaProducer<String, String>(producerConfig)) { List<Future<RecordMetadata>> acks = new ArrayList<>(); for (int seq = 0; seq < 1000; seq++) { String key = mode.equals("no-keys") ? null : "acct-" + (seq % 10 + 1); acks.add(producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>(TOPIC, key, seq + "," + "x".repeat(80)))); } for (Future<RecordMetadata> ack : acks) sentTo.add(ack.get().partition()); } System.out.printf("mode %s: 1000 records to %s (%d partitions)%n", mode, TOPIC, start.size()); System.out.println("in send order: " + runs(sentTo)); // 3. read them back from where this run started, in the order the consumer hands them out List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> seen = new ArrayList<>(); try (var consumer = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(common)) { consumer.assign(start.keySet()); start.forEach(consumer::seek); long deadline = System.nanoTime() + Duration.ofSeconds(15).toNanos(); while (seen.size() < 1000 && System.nanoTime() < deadline) { consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500)).forEach(seen::add); } } // 4. per key: which partitions, and did the consumer see that key's records in send order? Map<String, SortedSet<Integer>> partitions = new TreeMap<>(Comparator.comparingInt(k -> Integer.parseInt(k.substring(5)))); Map<String, Integer> lastSeq = new HashMap<>(); Set<String> outOfOrder = new HashSet<>(); for (var r : seen) { if (r.key() == null) continue; partitions.computeIfAbsent(r.key(), k -> new TreeSet<>()).add(r.partition()); int seq = seq(r); Integer prev = lastSeq.put(r.key(), seq); if (prev != null && seq < prev) outOfOrder.add(r.key()); } partitions.forEach((key, ps) -> System.out.printf(" %-8s partitions %-14s in send order: %s%n", key, ps, outOfOrder.contains(key) ? "no" : "yes")); // 5. and the stream as a whole? for (int i = 1; i < seen.size(); i++) { if (seq(seen.get(i)) < seq(seen.get(i - 1))) { System.out.printf("whole stream: out of send order at read #%d (seq %d came right after seq %d)%n", i, seq(seen.get(i)), seq(seen.get(i - 1))); return; } } System.out.println("whole stream: in send order"); } static int seq(ConsumerRecord<String, String> r) { return Integer.parseInt(r.value().substring(0, r.value().indexOf(','))); } /** "p3 x153, p0 x152, ..." : how many records in a row went to the same partition. */ static String runs(List<Integer> partitions) { List<String> out = new ArrayList<>(); int count = 1; for (int i = 1; i <= partitions.size(); i++) { if (i < partitions.size() && partitions.get(i).equals(partitions.get(i - 1))) { count++; } else { out.add("p" + partitions.get(i - 1) + " x" + count); count = 1; } } String shown = String.join(", ", out.subList(0, Math.min(8, out.size()))); return shown + (out.size() > 8 ? ", ..." : "") + " (" + out.size() + " runs)"; } }

Every account uses exactly one partition, and every account's 100 records came back in send order. The stream as a whole broke at the 100th record: the consumer handed out all of partition 2 first (acct-1, seq 0 to 990), then moved to partition 3, which starts with seq 5. Which partition comes first can differ on your run; the per-key lines will not. Partition 4 holds three accounts and partition 1 one: 10 keys spread unevenly.

sections.h: Records without a key go in sticky runs
sections.html:
Some records have no key: an audit event, a metrics sample, a log line. Any partition will do, so the producer is free to pick. What it picks decides how well the records batch.

A batch is a group of records for the same partition that travels in one request. The producer collects records per partition and sends each batch as a unit. Lesson 6 of this track opens the batching machinery; here you only need the effect: a request carrying 100 records costs about the same as a request carrying one.

Before Kafka 2.4, a record without a key went to the next partition in turn. That spread perfectly and batched badly: with 6 partitions, consecutive records went to six different batches, so each batch filled six times slower and many requests carried one or two records.

Kafka 2.4 (KIP-480) made the producer sticky: it kept sending to one partition until that partition's batch was full or sent, then picked another. Batches got bigger, but a new problem showed up. A slow broker sends its batches later, so its partitions stayed "current" longer and collected more records, which made the broker slower still. KIP-794's test showed one broker receiving about 46.8 MB while each of the other two got about 9 MB.

Kafka 3.3 (KIP-794) fixed the rule. The producer now switches partitions after a fixed amount of data: between batch.size bytes (16 KB by default) and twice that, at a batch boundary when it can. It picks the next partition at random, weighted against partitions with long queues, so a slow broker gets less new data instead of more. That weighting is partitioner.adaptive.partitioning.enable, on by default. With partitioner.availability.timeout.ms (0, off, by default) the producer can also skip a partition whose broker stops answering.

None of this applies to keyed records. A keyed record goes to its hash partition even when that partition's leader is down; it waits, retries and, if the leader stays away, fails with a timeout. Kafka will not move an account's payment to another partition to save time, because that would break the account's order. If you want keyed records spread like unkeyed ones, partitioner.ignore.keys=true does it: the key is still stored with the record, and per-key order is gone.

The producer stayed on one partition for about 350 records, about 32 KB: twice batch.size. It may switch after 16 KB only when that partition's open batch is exactly full, which rarely lines up, so it usually runs on to the 2x cap. The last run is longer only because the demo stopped. sections.h: Choose the key, then keep the partition count
sections.html:
The key decides two things at once: what stays in order, and how evenly the work spreads. Pick it for the order you need, then check the spread.

For payments the account id is usually right. Every change to one balance stays in order, and a large bank has hundreds of thousands of accounts, so partitions fill evenly. The payment id spreads even better and keeps one payment's authorization, capture and refund together, but two payments on one account can then be processed in either order. The merchant id looks natural for a settlement topic and is often a trap. If one merchant brings 30% of all payments, its partition gets 30% of the records, and the one consumer that reads it does several times the work of the others. Adding consumers doesn't help: a partition is read by one consumer per group. A key that concentrates traffic like this is a hot key, the same problem the Partitioning track met with database shards.

The other half of the rule is the partition count. The hash is fixed, but the remainder depends on the number you divide by. Grow accounts from 6 to 8 partitions and acct-1 moves from partition 2 to partition 6. Most keys move. A key stays only if its hash gives the same remainder for 6 and for 8, which holds for 6 of every 24 hash values, so about three keys in four change partition. The lab checks that number on 10,000 keys. This is the weakness of hash modulo N that the Partitioning track's lesson on consistent hashing fixed for databases; Kafka's producer still uses plain modulo, so the partition count of a keyed topic is effectively fixed.

A moved key breaks its own ordering. Records of acct-1 written before the change are in partition 2, newer ones go to partition 6, and a consumer of partition 6 that is caught up processes the new records while partition 2's consumer is still behind on the old ones. A running producer also keeps the old partition count until it refreshes its metadata (metadata.max.age.ms, 5 minutes by default), so for a while two producers can put one key in two places. And the consumer docs warn that a consumer with auto.offset.reset=latest can silently skip records written to the new partitions before it notices them.

So decide the count up front, with room for a few years of growth; lesson 11 of this track covers sizing. If you must grow a keyed topic, stop the producers, let the consumers finish, add the partitions, then restart. Or create a new topic with more partitions and move to it.

try.title: Grow the topic and watch the keys move
steps: Run PartitionForDemo for all ten accounts and note each partition: add -Pargs='acct-1 acct-2 acct-3 acct-4 acct-5 acct-6 acct-7 acct-8 acct-9 acct-10' to the command from the first Try-it.
Grow the topic to 8 partitions with the command below. Predict how many of the ten accounts will move, then run the same demo command again.
Run KeyOrderDemo once more. It reads only this run's records, so each account shows one partition again: the new one for the five that moved (acct-1 partitions [6]).
Stop the broker from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml down -v.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.html: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh \ --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --alter --topic accounts --partitions 8

try.expect:
Before, with 6 partitions, the ten accounts were in partitions 2, 5, 5, 4, 0, 3, 4, 1, 0, 4. After (trimmed to the first and last lines):

topic accounts has 8 partitions
key            murmur2    positive   % 8   producer chose
acct-1       294059390   294059390     6   partition 6
acct-2      2084802707  2084802707     3   partition 3
...
acct-10      981674020   981674020     4   partition 4

The hashes didn't change; only the divisor did. Five of the ten moved (acct-1, acct-2, acct-3, acct-6, acct-9) and five stayed (acct-4, acct-5, acct-7, acct-8, acct-10). Over many keys about three in four move; ten keys is a small sample. Every record those five accounts wrote before the change is still in its old partition.

analogy: Think of a mail room with six pigeonholes. Every clerk who drops off a letter works out the hole from the account number with the same sum, so all letters for one account end up in the same hole, stacked in the order they arrived. Whoever empties a hole reads its letters top to bottom, in order. Nobody can say whether a letter in hole 2 came before one in hole 5, and nobody needs to. The analogy breaks in two places. The sum is done by every sender, not by the mail room, so a sender who uses a different sum puts letters in the wrong hole. And adding two holes changes the sum, so most accounts get a new hole while their old letters stay in the old one.
world: Your payment service should set the account id as the key on every event about a balance: ProducerRecord("payments", accountId, event), or Record.of(accountId, event) with a Quarkus emitter. Then authorizations, captures and refunds for one account reach your ledger consumer in the order they were sent. Watch two things in review. A Python or Go service using librdkafka on the same topic must set partitioner=murmur2_random, or it sends the same account to a different partition than your Java services. And a request to "just add partitions" to a keyed topic is a migration, not a config change: plan it like one, or size the topic for growth on day one.
mistake: Adding partitions to a busy keyed topic to fix consumer lag. The topic has 6 partitions, the consumers are behind, and someone runs kafka-topics.sh --alter --partitions 12 to add consumers. It works for throughput, and half the accounts silently move to new partitions. Their newest events are processed by idle consumers on the new partitions while the old events still wait in the lagging ones, so captures overtake authorizations and balances go briefly wrong. The mistake is easy because the command succeeds and nothing logs a warning. The fix is to choose the count up front, and when you must grow, drain first or move to a new topic.

compare.title: Send a keyed payment and see where it went, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: var record = new ProducerRecord<>("payments", payment.accountId(), payment.toJson()); producer.send(record, (md, e) -> { if (e != null) { log.error("send failed for {}", payment.accountId(), e); } else { log.debug("{} -> partition {} offset {}", payment.accountId(), md.partition(), md.offset()); } });

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: val record = ProducerRecord("payments", payment.accountId, payment.toJson()) producer.send(record) { md, e -> if (e != null) { log.error("send failed for {}", payment.accountId, e) } else { log.debug("{} -> partition {} offset {}", payment.accountId, md.partition(), md.offset()) } }

compare.note: The key is the second constructor argument in both; leave it out (or pass null) and the record goes in a sticky run instead. Kotlin passes the Callback as a trailing lambda, because Callback is a Java interface with one method. The callback runs on the producer's network thread once the broker has answered, so keep it short: log or count, never block. Both versions infer the generic types from the arguments, and both hash payment.accountId with murmur2 when the record is sent.

worked.title: Measure how evenly a key spreads before you choose it

steps.say: The settlement team wants to key settlements by merchant id, on 12 partitions. Before agreeing, take a day's sample of keys (here a list of 100,000 merchant ids, one per payment) and count where the default partitioner would put each one. Utils is org.apache.kafka.common.utils.Utils.
steps.code: // 1. count records per partition, exactly as the producer would place them int[] perPartition = new int[12]; for (String merchant : sampleMerchantIds) { int p = Utils.toPositive(Utils.murmur2(merchant.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) % 12; perPartition[p]++; }

alt.html: // 1. count records per partition, exactly as the producer would place them val perPartition = IntArray(12) for (merchant in sampleMerchantIds) { val p = Utils.toPositive(Utils.murmur2(merchant.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8))) % 12 perPartition[p]++ }

steps.say: Turn the counts into one number: the busiest partition divided by the average. 1.0 is perfect. The busiest partition's consumer sets the pace for the whole group, so this ratio is roughly how much slower the group is than it would be with a perfect spread.
steps.code: // 2. skew = busiest partition / average partition double average = sampleMerchantIds.size() / 12.0; int busiest = Arrays.stream(perPartition).max().orElseThrow(); System.out.printf("skew %.2f%n", busiest / average);

alt.html: // 2. skew = busiest partition / average partition val average = sampleMerchantIds.size / 12.0 val busiest = perPartition.max() println("skew %.2f".format(busiest / average))

steps.say: Read the numbers. If one merchant has 30% of the payments, its partition alone holds 30,000 of 100,000 records against an average of about 8,333, so the skew is at least 3.6: one consumer does 3.6 times the average work and adding consumers changes nothing. Run the same count on account ids and you get close to 1.0, because no single account is a large share.

So key settlements by account id (or by payment id, if settlement only needs one payment's events in order), and let the settlement job group by merchant when it aggregates. Keep this check as a test: rerun it when the traffic mix changes.

lab.title: Write the key-to-partition rule and prove it on a real producer
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. 13 of 15 fail. The two that pass need no code from you: one checks the murmur2 you were given against Kafka's own, and one shows a real producer sending records without a key in long runs.

In KeyPartitioner.java, write toPositive, then partitionFor: UTF-8 bytes, murmur2, toPositive, remainder by the partition count. KeyPartitionerTest compares your answer with kafka-clients for 10,000 keys and six partition counts.
In KeyOrdering.kt, write keysOutOfOrder, firstGlobalBreak and partitionsByKey. KeyOrderingTest runs them on the six records from the stepper.
Write movedKeys with your partitionFor. The test expects about three keys in four to move from 6 to 8 partitions; its comment has the arithmetic.

Run everything. KeysOnBrokerTest sends 1,000 payments for 10 accounts into 6 partitions on a Kafka 4.4 broker and checks three things: the producer chose your partition for every record, each key came back in order, and the whole stream did not. Its last test grows a topic to 8 partitions and checks that exactly the keys from your movedKeys ended up in two partitions.
hints: number & 0x7fffffff clears the top bit and keeps the rest. Math.abs gives a different partition for most negative hashes, and Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is still negative.
Hash the bytes, not the String: key.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8). The test includes "é", which is one char and two bytes.
In Kotlin, groupBy({ it.key!! }, { it.partition }) maps each key to the list of its partitions; .mapValues { (_, ps) -> ps.toSet() } turns each list into a set. Filter out null keys first.

drill.title: Place a key from memory
drill.prompt: Write partitionFor(String key, int numPartitions) from memory, in Java or Kotlin, using Utils.murmur2. Then work out by hand: acct-17 hashes to -1871546916. (a) Which partition of 6 does it get? (b) Which partition would Math.abs give? Compare with the answer.

answer.html: static int partitionFor(String key, int numPartitions) { byte[] bytes = key.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8); // what StringSerializer sends return (Utils.murmur2(bytes) & 0x7fffffff) % numPartitions; } // (a) -1871546916 & 0x7fffffff = 2^31 - 1871546916 = 275936732; 275936732 % 6 = 2 // (b) Math.abs gives 1871546916; 1871546916 % 6 = 0. Wrong: the producer puts acct-17 in partition 2.

alt.html: fun partitionFor(key: String, numPartitions: Int): Int { val bytes = key.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8) // what StringSerializer sends return (Utils.murmur2(bytes) and 0x7fffffff) % numPartitions } // (a) -1871546916 and 0x7fffffff = 2^31 - 1871546916 = 275936732; 275936732 % 6 = 2 // (b) abs gives 1871546916; 1871546916 % 6 = 0. Wrong: the producer puts acct-17 in partition 2.

recap: The producer picks the partition, before the record leaves your JVM. For a keyed record it computes (murmur2(key bytes) & 0x7fffffff) % partitions.
The same key always lands in the same partition, so records with one key keep the order in which they reached the leader. Across partitions there is no order.
Records without a key go in sticky runs: since Kafka 3.3 (KIP-794) the producer switches partition after about batch.size to twice batch.size bytes, favouring partitions with short queues.
Key payments by account id for per-account order and an even spread. A hot key, such as a merchant with 30% of traffic, overloads one partition and its one consumer.
Growing a topic from 6 to 8 partitions moves about three keys in four, and their old records stay behind. Choose the count up front, or drain before you grow.
Other clients may hash differently: librdkafka defaults to CRC32 and needs partitioner=murmur2_random to match Java.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "Kafka keeps our payment events in order." Explain exactly which order Kafka keeps, how the key fits in, and two things that would break it.
explain.answer: Kafka keeps order inside a partition and nowhere else. The producer hashes each record's key with murmur2 and takes the remainder by the partition count, so every event for one account, keyed by account id, lands in the same partition and is read in the order it reached the leader. Events for different accounts sit in different partitions with no order between them, which is fine because we only need each account's history in order. Two things break it. If the key isn't the account id, or is missing, one account's events spread over several partitions and a capture can be processed before its authorization. And if someone adds partitions, most accounts hash to a new partition while their older events are still in the old one, so new events can overtake old ones. Two service instances racing on the same account also land in arrival order, not business order.

deeper.html:
The partitioner is a plugin point. partitioner.class takes any class that implements org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Partitioner, whose partition(topic, key, keyBytes, value, valueBytes, cluster) returns a partition number; the producer rejects a negative one. Kafka ships RoundRobinPartitioner, but its own docs warn it can spread records unevenly (KAFKA-9965). Write your own only when the default really can't express the rule, for example to pin a few known hot merchants to dedicated partitions. Every producer and every stream job that joins on the key must then use the same class.

That last point matters for Kafka Streams (the Stream processing track's Kafka Streams lesson). A join between two topics needs them co-partitioned: the same number of partitions and the same key-to-partition rule, so that acct-17 is in partition 2 of both. Streams uses the same murmur2 rule as the producer by default, which is why a topic written by a librdkafka client with default settings can't be joined correctly with one written from Java.

One more detail of the sticky rule. The producer counts the bytes it has handed to the current partition. After batch.size bytes it switches only if that partition's open batch is full at that moment, so the switch lands on a batch boundary; after twice batch.size it switches regardless. An exact fit is rare, which is why the Try-it's runs were about 32 KB, the 2x cap. KIP-794 explains the trade: a switch in the middle of a batch would leave a small batch behind on the old partition.
